These results confirm that generational depth signatures generalize across architectures and are not an artifact of generator identity.

To isolate the depth signal from generator identity, we train a binary classifier (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+) on each of the eight generators independently and evaluate on all others.
Table~\ref{tab:transfer} reports the full 8$\times$8 transfer matrix and Figure~\ref{fig:transfer} visualizes it as a heatmap.
Note that these classifiers are trained with a binary objective, whereas the LOGO classifiers in Table~\ref{tab:logo-results} are trained on a 3-class task and evaluated on the binary subtask; the two setups are therefore not directly comparable.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\scriptsize
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{3pt}
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{l|cccccccc}
\toprule
\textbf{Train $\backslash$ Test} & \textbf{Py-2.8B} & \textbf{Py-1B} & \textbf{Qw-0.6B} & \textbf{Qw-1.7B} & \textbf{Qw-8B} & \textbf{OLMo-1B} & \textbf{Ll-3B} & \textbf{Mi-7B} \\
\midrule
Py-2.8B  & \underline{0.985} & 0.873 & 0.823 & 0.833 & 0.741 & 0.829 & 0.815 & 0.712 \\
Py-1B    & 0.834 & \underline{0.987} & 0.828 & 0.821 & 0.704 & 0.778 & 0.764 & 0.620 \\
Qw-0.6B  & 0.786 & 0.846 & \underline{0.991} & 0.851 & 0.786 & 0.795 & 0.760 & 0.680 \\
Qw-1.7B  & 0.794 & 0.839 & 0.859 & \underline{0.989} & 0.790 & 0.817 & 0.798 & 0.717 \\
Qw-8B   & 0.811 & 0.836 & 0.853 & 0.855 & \underline{0.984} & 0.848 & 0.839 & 0.790 \\
OLMo-1B  & 0.811 & 0.827 & 0.837 & 0.852 & 0.803 & \underline{0.988} & 0.828 & 0.763 \\
Ll-3B    & 0.856 & 0.860 & 0.845 & 0.851 & 0.798 & 0.851 & \underline{0.987} & 0.787 \\
Mi-7B    & 0.834 & 0.837 & 0.837 & 0.845 & 0.817 & 0.849 & 0.851 & \underline{0.969} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\caption{Cross-generator binary F1 transfer matrix (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+). Each row trains on one generator; each column evaluates on another. Diagonal entries (\underline{underlined}) are within-generator. All 56 off-diagonal pairs exceed chance (0.5). Classifiers use the same 7-feature XGBoost configuration as LOGO but are trained with a binary objective.}
\label{tab:transfer}
\end{table}

\begin{figure}[h]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig_transfer_heatmap.pdf}
\caption{Heatmap of the cross-generator binary F1 transfer matrix (Table~\ref{tab:transfer}). Same-family pairs (e.g., Pythia$\leftrightarrow$Pythia, Qwen$\leftrightarrow$Qwen) show slightly higher transfer; Mi-7B is the hardest transfer target (column minimum 0.62) yet remains well above chance.}
\label{fig:transfer}
\end{figure}

All 56 off-diagonal transfer pairs yield F1 above chance, with a mean of 0.810 (95\% bootstrap CI [0.796, 0.822]; one-sample $t=46.58$, $p < 10^{-10}$).
Transfer is strongest within families (e.g., Py-2.8B$\to$Py-1B: 0.87) and weakest for Py-1B$\to$Mi-7B (0.62), consistent with the scale and reference-affinity effects discussed in \S\ref{sec:results-differential}.
These results confirm that depth signatures generalize across architectures, parameter scales, and model families, ruling out generator identity as a primary confound.

2	\label{sec:limitations}

4	All eight generators are base (pretrained) models.

7	Preliminary instruct experiments confirm that depth signal degrades substantially under instruction tuning: OLMo-2-1B-Instruct drops to 3-class LOGO F1\,=\,0.338 (vs.\ 0.763 base; this is classification F1, distinct from the clustering silhouette of the same value reported in \S\ref{sec:discussion}) and Qwen3-0.6B with chat template to 0.667 (vs.\ 0.816 base); these comparisons use earlier LOGO subsets (5--6 generators) predating the full 8-generator expansion in Table~\ref{tab:logo-results}.

# OpenReview Submission Form — Draft Text

## TL;DR (max 250 characters)

We show recursive LLM generation produces structured distributional drift, enabling ordinal depth classification (gen-0/gen-1/gen-2+) via a 7-feature ensemble under leave-one-generator-out evaluation across eight base models.

(Characters: ~213)

## Abstract (plain text, no LaTeX)

Text generated by large language models (LLMs) increasingly re-enters the web and seeds subsequent generation, producing recursive chains that progressively diverge from human-written text. As such text contaminates training corpora, distinguishing generation depth from binary authorship becomes important for data provenance. We study this phenomenon in base (pretrained) models and ask whether the drift is structured enough to classify how many generation steps a text has undergone, framing this as generation depth classification (gen-0/gen-1/gen-2+ rather than binary real-vs-synthetic). Across eight base models from five families (0.6B-8B parameters), we identify a differential depth response (DDR): features partition into drifting, intermediate, and near-stationary groups, consistent with recursive generation shifting the negative log-likelihood (NLL) location under a reference model while distributional shape remains stable. A 7-feature ensemble achieves leak-free binary F1 = 0.694 under leave-one-generator-out evaluation, generalizing across model families. The depth signal degrades substantially under instruction tuning, restricting current applicability to base models.

(Words: ~149)
